children: 0556 GMT - Some form of a deal between the U.S. and Iran is still likely before the U.S. midterm elections in November, Jefferies' Mohit Kumar says in a note. "We are still optimistic that we would have some sort of a deal before the mid-terms," the global economist says. From Iran's perspective, President Trump is likely to be ready to give more concessions before the midterms, while from Trump's perspective, if he can secure a deal before the midterms, "it could potentially help in the odds for the Senate which is currently looking too close to call," Kumar says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0554 GMT - Norges Bank is expected to aim for an early September date for its planned syndication of a new 20-year government bond due to its upcoming rate decision on Sept. 24 and the autumn school holiday in Norway, SEB's Erica Dalsto says in a note. Norges Bank has previously said it aims to issue between 5 billion kroner and 10 billion Norwegian kroner in September or October. "We expect it to aim for the maximum amount, which has been the case in earlier syndications this year," the chief Norway strategist says. Norges Bank has issued 81 billion kroner in bonds, including Wednesday's auction, while the annual borrowing interval is 100 billion kroner to 110 billion kroner. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0537 GMT - The super El Nino event should have a milder impact on Thailand's economy and headline inflation compared with the last one in 2015-2016, Maybank economists say in a report. A prolonged stretch of hotter, drier weather would crimp output in Thailand's agricultural sector. However, fresh produce accounts for 8% of the CPI basket, down from around 10% in 2015-2016, they note. The economy is also increasingly driven by the electronics and digital sectors, making it less exposed to lower agricultural output. Maybank expects Thailand's 2026 and 2027 GDP growth of 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively. It projects headline inflation to average 1.6% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0527 GMT - The prospect of the Federal Reserve following through on Chairman Kevin Warsh's hawkish message at Jackson Hole at the September meeting, together with the potential for further Treasury interventions, makes it challenging to hold long-end steepeners outright over the next few weeks, Deutsche Bank strategists say in a note. Longer term and more structurally, however, the strategists continue to favor higher term premia and steepener expressions, they say. These views are "based on negative underlying fundamentals and our view that meaningful fiscal consolidation remains unlikely," they say. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0521 GMT - Higher energy prices contributed to the recent bond selloff but the market isn't in panic mode, Allianz Research analysts say in a note. "Renewed tensions in the Middle East since July and destructions of refining capacity in Russia have raised energy costs in particular gas prices again, leading to higher inflation and central bank expectations (Federal Reserve terminal rate +35bp, European Central Bank +50bp) explaining the lion's share of rate increases," they say. While sovereign bond yields have risen since July, again reaching multi-year highs, the speed of increase was lower than after the start of the U.S.-Iran war, they say. "Bond markets are still functioning well according to bid-ask spreads or auction demand, but elevated rate levels are rightfully raising debt sustainability concerns." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0511 GMT - Investors are repricing sovereign debt from the U.S. to Europe and Japan as they adjust to a world of structurally higher inflation, larger government deficits and higher neutral interest rates, BondBloxx's JoAnne Bianco says in a note. "The story on government debt might be 'higher for a lot longer' instead of just 'higher for longer'," the senior investment strategist says. The continued sell-off in bonds isn't solely about inflation, she says. "Investors are demanding a higher term premium to hold long-dated government bonds" as concerns are growing about persistent fiscal deficits and elevated government borrowing needs. In addition, investors are being asked to absorb significantly more government debt issuance than they were a decade ago--and are demanding higher yields as compensation, she says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0507 GMT - The bond market outlook could get worse before it gets better, Allianz Research analysts say in a note. "While current yield levels look attractive, the negative feedback loop between higher rates and debt sustainability could trigger self-fulfilling prophecies in several countries," they say, pointing to France, Italy, U.K., Japan and the U.S. They estimate temporary yield spikes of up to 70 basis points before central banks would weigh in. "But overall, we consider risks as balanced as any demand side shock would rapidly lower yields." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0506 GMT - Investors are likely face a period of higher yields for longer, Vontobel's Christian Hantel says in note. The global bond sell-off continues on the back of renewed tensions between the U.S. and Iran and rising oil prices as a result, the portfolio manager says. Investors also seem to digest Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech at the Jackson Hole symposium and his more hawkish tone, he says. "As Warsh was very firm on bringing down inflation to the 2% target, he also emphasized that there could be more work to do to ultimately achieve this goal," he says. "So now we are likely to live with higher yields for longer." (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0503 GMT - Bitcoin edges up but is struggling to break out of its recent range below the $80,000 mark, as global yields' grim march higher keeps risk-off sentiment intact. Current market conditions aren't looking favorable for crypto: The bond selloff is raising an alarm about debt sustainability, and higher energy prices are fanning inflation worries. All these points to a higher-rate environment that dims the appeal of non-traditional assets. On a positive note, institutional demand for Bitcoin has shown resilience, says Milad Azar at XTB MENA. A sustained streak of ETF inflows could underpin the market, while major buyer Strategy's resumption of Bitcoin purchases after a prolonged pause supports sentiment. Inflation data, central bank meetings and crypto legislation progress in the U.S. will remain on the radar. Bitcoin is up 0.2% at $77,581. (fabiana.negrinochoa@wsj.com)

0447 GMT - Australia's GDP growth held up respectably in the June quarter, but its composition doesn't point to a re-accelerating economy, says Sunny Nguyen, Head of Australia Economics at Moody's Analytics. Private investment fell, consumers saved rather than spent, and net trade was positive only because people stopped traveling, Nguyen says in an email. While Moody's base case still has the Reserve Bank of Australia holding rates in September, Nguyen sees risk of a November hike as significantly higher. If the September-quarter trimmed mean inflation is at or above 0.9% on quarter, RBA will have little choice but to move the needle again, she adds.(monica.gupta@wsj.com)

0444 GMT - China's housing sentiment likely improved in August, according to BofA Securities in a research note. A BofA survey showed that 40% of respondents expect prices to rise in Tier 1 cities. "The latest Tier 1 recovery appears more genuine, accompanied by inventory drawdown and a recovery in rental yields," they note. That said, sentiment remains weak in Tier 2 cities and the improvement elsewhere has been volatile, the bank says. Investors are watching for more clues on whether a durable recovery is taking hold across the broader housing market, BofA says. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0419 GMT - Asian currencies face headwinds from rising U.S. Treasury yields and oil prices, MUFG Bank's Lloyd Chan says in a research report. "Rising oil prices worsen the terms of trade for net energy importers such as Thailand, the Philippines, India, and Korea, while simultaneously boosting inflation expectations," the senior currency analyst says. Since the Jackson Hole economic policy symposium last Friday, Treasury yields have surged across the curve, Chan notes. Also, Brent crude oil price jumped 4.6% Tuesday to nearly $95 per barrel after renewed strikes between the U.S. and Iran, Chan adds. The dollar edges 0.1% higher to 33.32 baht and rises 0.3% to 62.609 pesos, LSEG data show.(ronnie.harui@wsj.com)
